title: Battle of Chipyong-ni (1951): The 360-Degree Perimeter Defense
subtitle: Feb 13 – 15, 1951

lines: The night of February 13th, 1951. Chipyong-ni, Gyeonggi Province.
Inside a small, snow-covered basin, about 5,600 American and French troops were trapped.
Every hill around them was packed with Chinese troops.
There was no way out. Chipyong-ni was an island, completely surrounded.
The Chinese command was certain.
Once again, they believed, the UN forces would break and run.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: For nearly three months since China entered the war, the UN had done nothing but retreat.
The surrounded force: the U.S. 23rd Infantry Regiment and the French Battalion.
Against them came several Chinese divisions, many times their number.

callouts.text: Strength varies by source · ROK records

lines: Yet three days later,
it was the Chinese who pulled back first.

visual.text:
Three days later,
who pulled back first?

lines: The place where China's human-wave tactics were first broken head-on.
This is the story of the 'Gettysburg of the Korean War': the Battle of Chipyong-ni.
In October 1950, China entered the war.
UN forces lost Seoul again and fell back as far as Pyeongtaek and Wonju.
On January 4th, 1951, Seoul fell once more, in what Koreans call the January 4th Retreat.
Among the troops spread a fear that the Chinese simply could not be beaten.
scenes.label: U.S. Marines rest by a snowy roadside (1951)

lines: Then came Lieutenant General Matthew Ridgway, the Eighth Army's new commander.
He resolved to stop retreating and meet the Chinese head-on.
scenes.label: Matthew Ridgway (1951)

lines: On February 11th, 1951, the Chinese launched another major offensive.
As the line near Hoengseong collapsed, the Chipyong-ni force was left jutting out alone.
Chipyong-ni was a crossroads to Yangpyeong, Yeoju, and Wonju, on the Jungang rail line.
Lose it, and the entire central front could start to crumble.

callouts.text: Roads + Railway = Key to the Central Front

lines: But the terrain was as bad as it gets.
The village sat in a basin about 100 meters above sea level, ringed by hills of 300 to 400 meters.
On the morning of February 13th, the corps commander ordered a withdrawal.
But that same day, Ridgway overruled him. Chipyong-ni would be held.
In early February, this regiment had already fought the Chinese near the Twin Tunnels, southeast of Chipyong-ni.
The survivors of that fight now dug in again at Chipyong-ni.
The regimental commander, Colonel Paul Freeman, made his call.
Without the men to hold the high ridges, he built a tight ring on the low hills around the village.
scenes.label: Paul Freeman (later, as a general)

lines: A circular perimeter, a little over a mile across.
1st Battalion took the north, 3rd the east, 2nd the south, and the French Battalion the west.
The French Battalion holding the west was led by Lieutenant Colonel Monclar.
A three-star general who demoted himself to lead a battalion in Korea, he was 59 years old.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: A veteran of both World Wars, he had about 800 French soldiers at his side.
scenes.label: The French Battalion in Korea (Apr 1951)

lines: February 13th, 10 p.m.
Out of the darkness came the sound of bugles, whistles, and gongs.
The Chinese struck from the northwest, the north, and the southeast at once.
Soon, the perimeter was under attack from every direction.
When the front rank fell, another surged forward behind it.
This was China's so-called human-wave assault.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The artillery at the center of the ring fired without pause.
Inside a surrounded circle, every direction was the front line.
scenes.label: 155mm howitzer firing (Korean War)

lines: On the night of February 14th, the Chinese came back in even greater numbers.
Starting near midnight, they hammered the north, then the east, then the west.
On February 14th, Colonel Freeman himself was hit in the leg by mortar fragments.
Still, he limped from position to position and never stopped commanding.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Ammunition began to run dangerously low.
Overhead, transport planes dropped ammunition crates by parachute.
Some men who left their foxholes to grab the crates were cut down by snipers.
scenes.label: Troops receiving airdropped supplies (1951)

lines: The most famous moment came in the west, on the French Battalion's line.
Answering the Chinese bugles, the French sounded sirens, fixed bayonets, and charged.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Faced with strange sounds and charging bayonets, the Chinese ranks scattered.
After hand-to-hand fighting, the western line held to the end.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: That night, Company I of the 3rd Battalion was the first position to be breached,
but its men counterattacked and retook it at once.
Dawn, February 15th.
At last, in the south, Company G's position collapsed.

chapter.title: THE SOUTH FALLS, THE TANKS COME

lines: The Chinese poured down from Hill 397 and drove into the southern perimeter.
The Ranger company counterattacked, but was thrown back after brutal hand-to-hand combat.
Private Bruno Orig of Company G stayed alone on his machine gun until his comrades got clear.
He was killed where he stood, and later received the Medal of Honor.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Sergeant Sitman of Company M threw himself on a grenade, saving five of his men.
At Chipyong-ni alone, two soldiers earned the Medal of Honor.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: That afternoon, a relief force set out from Yeoju to the south.
It was an armored column of 23 tanks under Colonel Crombez, commander of the 5th Cavalry Regiment.
Clinging to the tanks were some 160 infantrymen.
As they passed through Koksu-ri, gunfire rained down from the hills on both sides.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: The tanks kept rolling without stopping, and many infantrymen were left behind on the road.
When the column reached Chipyong-ni, only 23 riders were still aboard.

visual.note: TF Crombez infantry riders · U.S. records (Feb 15, 1951)

lines: Around 5 p.m., the tanks finally rolled into the Chipyong-ni perimeter.
With the ring broken, the Chinese began withdrawing to the north.
In the clearing skies, fighter-bombers hammered the encircling forces,
and the three-day siege was over.
scenes.label: U.S. Air Force ground attack (Korean War)

lines: How did some 5,000 surrounded men hold off an enemy many times their size?
Let's break it down into four factors.

visual.head: One Ring — How Did It Hold?

lines: First, the circular perimeter.
Because the ring was small and tight, reserves inside could rush to any breach.
And from the center, the artillery could swing its guns in any direction.
Second, firepower and the sky.
Transports made twenty-four ammunition drops,
and once the skies cleared, fighter-bombers pounded the ring of attackers.
scenes.label: F-51 Mustang fighter-bomber (Korean War)

lines: Third, leaders who refused to fall back.
Ridgway chose to hold instead of retreat,
while the wounded Freeman and 59-year-old Monclar fought beside their men.
Fourth, the armored relief.
Crombez's tanks tore through the encirclement without stopping.
It came at a heavy cost, but that breakthrough saved a perimeter on the brink.
scenes.label: Tanks supporting infantry (Korean War)

lines: U.S. records list UN losses at 51 killed, 250 wounded, and 42 missing.
Chinese casualties are estimated at about 5,000, though Chinese sources give just over 900.
For the first time since entering the war, the Chinese had clearly been beaten in battle.
Even the Chinese command later admitted it had underestimated its enemy.
A week later, Ridgway struck back with Operation Killer.
By March, Seoul was retaken, and the UN pushed back up to the 38th Parallel.
Today, Chipyong-ni is home to a battle memorial hall and a monument to the French troops.
scenes.label: French Battalion monument at Chipyong-ni

lines: Every February, ceremonies here honor the victory and the sacrifices of those days.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: A small circle, just a mile across, drawn in a snowy basin.
That circle changed the course of the war.
scenes.label: 1st Lt. Winget at Chipyong-ni (Feb 1951)

lines: One surrounded ring.
And those who held it to the end were the ones who would not step back, even with nowhere left to go.

items.text: One ring changed the course of the war
Nowhere to retreat — and they didn't
